title: Back to the future of skyscraper design

paragraphs.text: We are facing a crisis in building design. As global temperatures continue to rise, we are going to squander more and more energy on keeping our buildings mechanically cool until we have run out of capacity.

The only solution is a sweeping reinvention of how skyscrapers and major public buildings are designed. Some architects believe it is possible to accommodate natural ventilation and cooling in large buildings like these by looking into the past, before the widespread introduction of air-conditioning systems, which were relentlessly and aggressively promoted by 20th-century entrepreneurs.

The majority of contemporary buildings have absolutely no resilience to climate at all. To make them habitable, you have to seal them from the outside atmosphere and air condition them. The energy use and carbon emissions this generates are spectacular and to a large extent unnecessary. Buildings in the West count for 40-50% of electricity usage, generating substantial carbon emissions. The rest of the world is catching up at a frightening rate. Modern buildings cannot survive unless hard-wired to a life-support machine, yet this obsession with glass, steel and air-conditioned high-rise buildings continues; they are becoming status symbols around the world on an increasingly vast scale.

Architects working in the 19th and early 20th centuries had sophisticated methods of ventilating buildings. Of particular interest are the designs of John Shaw Billings for the first Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, USA, which opened in 1889. A research team recently spent three years digitally modelling Billings' designs. They put pathogens in the airstreams to model what would have happened if someone with tuberculosis (TB) was coughing in the wards, and they found the hospital's ventilation systems would have kept the other patients safe from harm. The researchers discovered that 19th-century hospital wards could generate up to 24 air changes an hour – that's similar to the performance of a modern-day, computer-controlled operating theatre – and they believe that wards based on these principles could be built for hospitals now.

Much of the ingenuity present in 19th-century hospital design was driven by a panicked public clamouring for buildings that could protect against what were known as 'miasmas' – toxic air that was believed to spread disease. Miasmas were considered lethal by most people, and were believed to explain the cholera outbreaks in London and Paris during the 1850s. Miasma theory attracted the attention of influential figures in medicine such as Florence Nightingale*. She believed that foul air, rather than germs, was the main cause of what was referred to at the time as 'hospital fever', leading to disease and frequent death. The prosperous steered clear of hospitals.

While these ideas have been long since disproved, it may now be time for a return to some of the building design principles that were associated with it. To go forward into our new low-energy, low-carbon future, we would be well advised to look back at design before our high-energy, high-carbon buildings appeared. What is surprising is how rich a legacy we have abandoned. In a similar way, we have seen how the widespread introduction of affordable antibiotics to fight infection, and the related relaxation in the ferocious cleanliness regimes in hospitals, have had frightening consequences which are only emerging now.

A series of buildings has recently been designed and built by a team led by Professor Alan Short which reinvent some of these ideas, including the iconic Queen's Building at De Montfort University in Leicester. This is naturally ventilated, passively cooled and naturally lit throughout. Conventional wisdom in the ventilation and heating industry was that this omission of mechanical and electrical equipment was impossible. Confounding its critics, the building was awarded Green Building of the Year in 1995 and was at the time the largest naturally ventilated building in Europe, influencing guidance in Europe and the USA.

Following this success, Short and his associates have also experimented with theatre design, including the Contact Theatre in Manchester, which uses the abundant heat sources of theatre lights and audience to drive air flows around the building. They also designed the passive downdraught-cooled School of Slavonic and East European Studies in London.

Short contends that glass skyscrapers in London and around the world will become a liability over the next 20 or 30 years if the expected rises in global temperatures and energy prices come to pass. He is convinced that skyscrapers cooled using the natural environment can be produced in almost any climate. He and his team have worked on hybrid buildings in the harsh climates of Beijing and Chicago, built with natural ventilation assisted by back-up air-conditioning which can be switched off on milder days and during the spring and autumn. 'I think you can upscale these designs,' he says, 'As you go higher, airspeeds increase and it becomes easier to control the climate within tall buildings.'

Short believes there are compelling reasons to reimagine the cities, offices and homes of the future. When discussing UK hospitals, he says, 'The Department of Health says new hospitals should be naturally ventilated, but they are not. Maybe it's time we changed our outlook.'

questions.prompt: Maintaining low temperatures in buildings will require increasing amounts of energy in the future.
The use of air-conditioning was encouraged in the last century for commercial reasons.
Energy can be saved if buildings are sealed from the outside atmosphere.
Air-conditioning in modern buildings can be dangerous to the health of those who live or work in them.

questions.prompt: When describing the 19th-century hospital designs of John Shaw Billings, the writer is impressed by

options.text: how simple they are in their design.
the impact they had on the treatment of tuberculosis.
how appropriate they are for modern health needs.
the influence they had on 20th-century hospital architecture.

questions.prompt: What point does the writer make about miasma theory?

options.text: It was rejected at the time by hospital staff.
It had a positive impact on hospital architecture.
It led to a decline in standards of public health.
It was successfully applied to control cholera.

questions.prompt: The writer refers to 'affordable antibiotics' to make the point that present hospital design

options.text: has led to new developments in drugs.
makes it difficult to fulfil requirements for cleanliness.
may be causing more problems than it solves.
has been negatively affected by cost-cutting measures.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about the use of natural ventilation in the Queen's Building at De Montfort University?

options.text: Specialists did not believe it would be effective.
It replaced the previous system of ventilation used there.
The award for this led to considerable controversy.
It did not follow the usual European or American guidelines.

questions.prompt: What is illustrated by the reference to buildings in Beijing and Chicago?

options.text: the need to educate people to depend less on air-conditioning
the special problems involved in climate control in high buildings
the difficulty of designing buildings for extreme weather conditions
the possibility of combining natural ventilation with other types of systems
